statement: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $F\colon A^{\mathbb Z}\to A^{\mathbb Z}$ a map of the full [shift space](c:shift-space) with the [product topology](c:product-topology). If $F$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and commutes with the shift $\sigma$, then $F$ is a [sliding block code](c:sliding-block-code). Conversely, every sliding block code is continuous and commutes with $\sigma$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet $A$ is finite and carries the [discrete topology](c:discrete-topology).
The map $F$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) for the product topology on $A^{\mathbb Z}$.
The map $F$ commutes with the shift: $F\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ F$.

conclusion: Some radius $r\ge0$ and local rule $\Phi\colon A^{2r+1}\to A$ give $F(x)_i=\Phi(x_{i-r},\dots,x_{i+r})$ for all $x$ and $i$, and conversely every such map is continuous and commutes with $\sigma$.

proofs.name: Compactness of the full shift
proofs.slogan: Compactness turns the continuity of one coordinate into a finite window, and shift-commutation moves that window everywhere.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $A\ne\emptyset$ and the full shift on $\mathbb Z$. For $\mathbb Z^d$ the same proof works with a box in place of $[-r,r]$.

roles.why: Finiteness of $A$ makes $A^{\mathbb Z}$ [compact](c:compact-space) and gives finitely many blocks.
Continuity makes the zero coordinate of $F(x)$ locally constant in $x$.
Shift-commutation carries the rule at coordinate $0$ to every coordinate $i$.

steps.slogan: Show that the zero coordinate of $F(x)$ is locally constant in $x$.
steps.detail: The map $g(x)=F(x)_0$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) into the finite [discrete](c:discrete-topology) set $A$. So each $x$ has a neighborhood where $g$ is constant. By the definition of the [product topology](c:product-topology), it contains a cylinder $\{y: y_{[-r_x,r_x]}=x_{[-r_x,r_x]}\}$.

steps.slogan: Choose one radius $r$ by a finite subcover of the compact space.
steps.detail: The space $A^{\mathbb Z}$ is [compact](c:compact-space) because $A$ is finite, so finitely many cylinders $C_1,\dots,C_m$ of step 1 cover it; let $r$ be the largest radius. If $x,y$ agree on $[-r,r]$ and $x\in C_j$, then $y\in C_j$, so $g(x)=g(y)$.

steps.slogan: Define the local rule $\Phi$ on the blocks of length $2r+1$.
steps.detail: For a block $w\in A^{2r+1}$, pick any $x$ with $x_{[-r,r]}=w$ and put $\Phi(w)=g(x)$. Step 2 shows that the value does not depend on $x$. Then $F(x)_0=\Phi(x_{-r},\dots,x_r)$ for all $x$.

steps.slogan: Move the rule to every coordinate by the shift.
steps.detail: Since $F\sigma^i=\sigma^iF$, we get $F(x)_i=(\sigma^iF(x))_0=F(\sigma^ix)_0=\Phi(x_{i-r},\dots,x_{i+r})$. So $F$ is the [sliding block code](c:sliding-block-code) of $\Phi$.

steps.slogan: Check that every sliding block code is continuous and shift-commuting.
steps.detail: A coordinate $F(x)_i$ depends only on $x_{i-r},\dots,x_{i+r}$, so it is continuous in the [product topology](c:product-topology). A map into a product is continuous when all its coordinates are. The index shift gives $F\sigma=\sigma F$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the characterization of sliding block codes.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 give the direct implication and step 5 gives the converse. So the sliding block codes are exactly the continuous maps of the full shift that commute with $\sigma$.

concepts.c:shift-space: The theorem describes maps of the full shift $A^{\mathbb Z}$.
concepts.c:product-topology: The topology of $A^{\mathbb Z}$ makes cylinders open and the space compact.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $F$ is the hypothesis that gives a finite window.
concepts.c:sliding-block-code: The conclusion says that $F$ is given by a finite-window local rule.
concepts.c:discrete-topology: The finite alphabet is discrete, so a continuous map into it is locally constant.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness yields one radius that works for all points.

source.note: G. A. Hedlund, Endomorphisms and automorphisms of the shift dynamical system, Math. Systems Theory 3 (1969) 320-375; also D. Lind and B. Marcus, An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding, Section 6.2.

statement: Let $G$ be a graph with any vertex set and let $c\ge1$ be an integer. If every finite subgraph of $G$ has a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring) with $c$ colors, then $G$ has one.

hypotheses.text: The number of colors $c$ is a finite positive integer.
Every finite subgraph of $G$ has a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring) with $c$ colors.

conclusion: The graph $G$ has a proper coloring with $c$ colors: adjacent vertices get different colors.

proofs.name: Compactness theorem of logic
proofs.slogan: Encode colorings as propositional clauses, satisfy every finite part by a finite subgraph, and apply the compactness theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for graphs of any cardinality. The clauses are finite because $c$ is finite.

roles.why: A finite number of colors gives finite clauses $\bigvee_{i<c}p_{v,i}$.
A finite set of clauses involves a finite vertex set, which carries a proper coloring.

steps.slogan: Encode a coloring by one propositional variable per vertex and color.
steps.detail: Take [propositional](c:propositional-logic) variables $p_{v,i}$ for each vertex $v$ and $i<c$, read as 'vertex $v$ has color $i$'. Let $T$ hold the clauses $\bigvee_{i<c}p_{v,i}$ for each $v$ and $\lnot p_{u,i}\lor\lnot p_{v,i}$ for each edge $uv$ and each $i<c$.

steps.slogan: Satisfy every finite set of clauses by coloring a finite subgraph.
steps.detail: A finite $T_0\subseteq T$ mentions only the variables of a finite vertex set $W$. By hypothesis the subgraph induced on $W$ has a proper coloring $f$. The assignment that makes $p_{v,i}$ true exactly when $f(v)=i$ satisfies $T_0$.

steps.slogan: Obtain one truth assignment that satisfies all clauses of $T$ at once.
steps.detail: By step 2 every finite subset of $T$ is satisfiable. The compactness theorem of propositional logic then gives an assignment that satisfies all of $T$.

steps.slogan: Read a proper coloring of $G$ off the truth assignment.
steps.detail: For each $v$ the first clause gives some $i$ with $p_{v,i}$ true; let $f(v)$ be the least such $i$. If $uv$ is an edge with $f(u)=f(v)=i$, both $p_{u,i}$ and $p_{v,i}$ are true, against an edge clause. So $f$ is proper.

concepts.c:graph-coloring: The proof builds a proper coloring of $G$ from colorings of finite parts.
concepts.c:propositional-logic: Colorability becomes the satisfiability of a set of propositional clauses.

source.note: The standard compactness argument for colorability of infinite graphs, with the usual propositional encoding of colors.

proofs.name: Tychonoff product of finite sets
proofs.slogan: Colorings form a compact product space, the proper-on-a-finite-set conditions are closed sets with the finite intersection property, so they share a point.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for graphs of any cardinality. It uses the axiom of choice through Tychonoff's theorem.

roles.why: Finitely many colors make each factor of the product finite, hence compact.
A proper coloring of the finite induced subgraph shows that finitely many conditions are compatible.

steps.slogan: Form the space of all colorings as a product of finite sets.
steps.detail: Let $X=\{0,\dots,c-1\}^V$ with the [product topology](c:product-topology) of the [discrete](c:discrete-topology) topology on each factor. Each factor is finite, so $X$ is [compact](c:compact-space) by Tychonoff's theorem.

steps.slogan: Define the closed set of colorings that are proper on a finite vertex set.
steps.detail: For finite $W\subseteq V$ let $F_W$ be the set of $f\in X$ with $f(u)\ne f(v)$ for every edge $uv$ inside $W$. The condition involves finitely many coordinates, so $F_W$ is [closed](c:closed-set).

steps.slogan: Show that the closed sets $F_W$ have the finite intersection property.
steps.detail: Let $W_1,\dots,W_k$ be finite and $W=\bigcup_jW_j$. By hypothesis the subgraph induced on $W$ has a proper coloring; extend it by color $0$ outside $W$. The result lies in $F_W\subseteq\bigcap_jF_{W_j}$.

steps.slogan: Pick a point in all sets $F_W$ and read it as a coloring.
steps.detail: In a compact space, closed sets with the [finite intersection property](c:finite-intersection-property) have a common point $f$. For every edge $uv$ we have $f\in F_{\{u,v\}}$, so $f(u)\ne f(v)$. Thus $f$ is a proper coloring of $G$ with $c$ colors.

concepts.c:graph-coloring: The point found in the intersection is a proper coloring of $G$.
concepts.c:product-topology: The product topology makes the space of all colorings compact.
concepts.c:discrete-topology: Each finite set of colors is discrete, so the factors are compact.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the coloring space gives a point in all the closed sets.
concepts.c:closed-set: The sets $F_W$ are closed, so compactness applies to them.
concepts.c:finite-intersection-property: This property of the family $F_W$ yields a common point.

source.note: The standard topological proof of the De Bruijn-Erdos theorem: compactness of a product of finite discrete spaces.

statement: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite [cardinal](c:cardinal-number), $\beth_0=\kappa$ and $\beth_{n+1}=2^{\beth_n}$. If the $(n+1)$-element subsets of a set $S$ with $|S|=\beth_n^{+}$ are colored with $\kappa$ colors, then some $H\subseteq S$ with $|H|=\kappa^{+}$ has all its $(n+1)$-element subsets of one color.

hypotheses.text: The number $\kappa$ is an infinite [cardinal](c:cardinal-number).
The number $n$ is a natural number.
The $(n+1)$-element subsets of a set $S$ of size $\beth_n^{+}$ are colored with $\kappa$ colors.

conclusion: Some $H\subseteq S$ of size $\kappa^{+}$ has all its $(n+1)$-element subsets of the same color.

proofs.name: Induction with an elementary submodel
proofs.slogan: Induct on $n$, and from a closed elementary submodel build a large end-homogeneous set to which the induction hypothesis applies.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in ZFC. The case $n=0$ is the base; for $n\ge1$ put $\lambda=\beth_{n-1}$, so $\beth_n=2^{\lambda}$, and assume the case $n-1$.

roles.why: The cardinal $\kappa^{+}$ is [regular](c:is-regular) and larger than the number of colors $\kappa$.
The number $n$ sets the length of the induction on the exponent $\beth_n$.
The coloring $F$ supplies the colors of the sets that the construction keeps.

steps.slogan: Prove the case $n=0$ by the pigeonhole principle.
steps.detail: A set of size $\kappa^{+}$ colored with $\kappa$ colors has a color class of size $\kappa^{+}$. Otherwise the set is a union of $\kappa$ sets of size at most $\kappa$, which has size at most $\kappa$, because $\kappa^{+}$ is a [regular cardinal](c:is-regular).

steps.slogan: Choose an elementary submodel of size $2^{\lambda}$ that is closed under $\lambda$-sequences.
steps.detail: Let $\theta=(2^{\lambda})^{+}$ and $F\colon[\theta]^{n+1}\to\kappa$. Take an [elementary substructure](c:elementary-substructure) $M$ of $H(\chi)$ with $F,\kappa,\theta\in M$, $|M|=2^{\lambda}$ and $M^{\lambda}\subseteq M$. It exists as a union of a chain of length $\lambda^{+}$ of hulls, since $(2^{\lambda})^{\lambda}=2^{\lambda}$.

steps.slogan: Place a point $\delta$ above $M$ and color the smaller sets by it.
steps.detail: Since $|M|<\theta$ and $\theta$ is regular, $M\cap\theta$ is bounded in $\theta$. Pick $\delta<\theta$ above it. Define $G(s)=F(s\cup\{\delta\})$ for $s\in[M\cap\theta]^{n}$.

steps.slogan: Build $\lambda^{+}$ increasing points whose later colors agree with $G$.
steps.detail: Choose $\alpha_\xi\in M$ for $\xi<\lambda^{+}$ above all $\alpha_\eta$ with $\eta<\xi$, so that $F(s\cup\{\alpha_\xi\})=G(s)$ for all $n$-subsets $s$ of $E_\xi=\{\alpha_\eta:\eta<\xi\}$. The set $E_\xi$ and $G\restriction[E_\xi]^{n}$ lie in $M$ by closure. The statement 'some $\beta$ above $E_\xi$ has $F(s\cup\{\beta\})=G(s)$ for all such $s$' is witnessed by $\delta$, so by elementarity some $\beta\in M$ witnesses it, and we call it $\alpha_\xi$.

steps.slogan: Apply the case $n-1$ to $G$ on the new set to get a homogeneous set.
steps.detail: The set $H_0=\{\alpha_\xi:\xi<\lambda^{+}\}$ has size $\beth_{n-1}^{+}$, so $G$ on $[H_0]^{n}$ has a homogeneous set $H$ of size $\kappa^{+}$. For $t\in[H]^{n+1}$ with largest point $\alpha_\xi$, $F(t)=G(t\setminus\{\alpha_\xi\})$, one common color. So $H$ is homogeneous for $F$.

concepts.c:cardinal-number: The theorem compares the sizes $\beth_n^{+}$ and $\kappa^{+}$ of infinite sets.
concepts.c:is-regular: Regularity of $\kappa^{+}$ and $\theta$ gives the pigeonhole step and the bound on $M$.
concepts.c:elementary-substructure: The elementary submodel lets the construction pick each new point inside $M$.

source.note: P. Erdos and R. Rado, A partition calculus in set theory, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 62 (1956) 427-489; the elementary submodel form of the proof is in T. Jech, Set Theory (3rd ed.), Chapter 9.

statement: Let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and let $\mu$ be a [measure](c:measure) on $\mathbb R$. Let $f$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the interval between $a$ and $b$, and let $g$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) for $\mu$ there with $g\ge0$ on $(\min(a,b),\max(a,b)]$. Then $\int_a^b fg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_a^b g\,d\mu$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $b$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed interval with ends $a$ and $b$.
The function $g$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) with respect to $\mu$ on the interval between $a$ and $b$.
The function $g$ is nonnegative on the half-open interval $(\min(a,b),\max(a,b)]$.

conclusion: Some $c$ between $a$ and $b$ satisfies $\int_a^b fg\,d\mu=f(c)\int_a^b g\,d\mu$.

proofs.name: Average value against a density
proofs.slogan: Turn $g\,d\mu$ into a measure $\nu$ and use that a continuous function on a connected set attains its $\nu$-average.
proofs.scope: All real $a,b$. The cases $a=b$ and $b<a$ reduce to $a<b$, and the case of zero total mass is treated separately.

roles.why: Continuity makes $f$ bounded, so $fg$ is integrable, and makes $f(s)$ an interval.
Integrability of $g$ makes $\nu$ a finite measure on $s$.
Nonnegativity of $g$ makes $\nu$ a positive measure, so averages stay inside the value range.

steps.slogan: Reduce to the case $a<b$ and the half-open interval $s=(a,b]$.
steps.detail: If $a=b$, both integrals vanish and $c=a$ works. If $b<a$, swap the ends: both integrals change sign and the interval is the same. For $a<b$ the integrals over $a..b$ are integrals over the connected set $s=(a,b]$.

steps.slogan: Replace the weight $g$ by the measure $\nu$ with density $g$ with respect to $\mu$.
steps.detail:
Since $g\ge0$ on $s$ and $g$ is integrable, $
u(E)=\int_Eg\,d\mu$ is a finite measure on $s$. The function $f$ is bounded on $[a,b]$, so $fg$ is integrable. Then $\int_sfg\,d\mu=\int_sf\,d
u$ and $\int_sg\,d\mu=
u(s)$.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $\nu(s)=0$ separately.
steps.detail: Then $g=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $s$. So $\int_sfg\,d\mu=0=f(c)\int_sg\,d\mu$ for any $c\in s$.

steps.slogan: If $\nu(s)>0$, show that the $\nu$-average of $f$ is a value of $f$ on $s$.
steps.detail:
The set $s$ is [connected](c:connected-space), so $f(s)$ is an interval by the intermediate value theorem; let $m=
u(s)^{-1}\int_sf\,d
u$. If $m

e0$, against the definition of $m$. Hence $m=f(c)$ for some $c\in s$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the average back to obtain the stated identity.
steps.detail: With $c$ from step 4, $\int_sfg\,d\mu=\int_sf\,d\nu=m\,\nu(s)=f(c)\int_sg\,d\mu$. Since $s\subseteq[a,b]$, the point $c$ lies between $a$ and $b$.

concepts.c:measure: The weight $g\,d\mu$ becomes a new measure $\nu$ on the interval.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ gives boundedness and an interval of values.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $g$ and of $fg$ makes both integrals finite.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of $(a,b]$ makes the image of $f$ an interval.

statement: Let $N$ and $T$ be bounded operators on a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), with $N$ [normal](c:normal-operator). If $TN=NT$, then $TN^*=N^*T$.

hypotheses.text: The operators $N$ and $T$ are bounded on a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$.
The operator $N$ is [normal](c:normal-operator): $NN^*=N^*N$.
The operator $T$ lies in the [commutant](c:commutant) of $N$: $TN=NT$.

conclusion: The operator $T$ also commutes with the adjoint: $TN^*=N^*T$.

proofs.name: Rosenblum's Liouville argument
proofs.slogan: Conjugate $T$ by a unitary family to get a bounded entire function, which is constant by Liouville, and differentiate it at $0$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for bounded $N$ and $T$ on a complex Hilbert space. Unbounded normal operators are not covered.

roles.why: The Hilbert space gives adjoints, unitary conjugation and the inner products used with Liouville.
Normality makes $N$ and $N^*$ commute, so the exponential of their combination factors.
Commutation with $N$ gives commutation with every exponential $e^{wN}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $T$ commutes with the exponential $e^{wN}$ for every complex $w$.
steps.detail: From $TN=NT$ we get $TN^k=N^kT$ for all $k$. The series $e^{wN}=\sum_kw^kN^k/k!$ converges in norm because $N$ is bounded. So $Te^{wN}=e^{wN}T$.

steps.slogan: Write $F(z)=e^{izN^*}Te^{-izN^*}$ as $U_zTU_z^{-1}$ with $U_z$ unitary.
steps.detail: Put $U_z=e^{i(zN^*+\bar zN)}$. The operator $zN^*+\bar zN$ is self-adjoint, so $U_z$ is [unitary](c:unitary-operator). Normality gives $U_z=e^{izN^*}e^{i\bar zN}$, and step 1 gives $U_zTU_z^{-1}=e^{izN^*}Te^{-izN^*}=F(z)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the operator norm of $F(z)$ equals $\|T\|$ for all $z$.
steps.detail: Unitary conjugation preserves the operator norm. So $\|F(z)\|=\|U_zTU_z^{-1}\|=\|T\|$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ is constant by Liouville's theorem.
steps.detail: For vectors $x,y$ the function $z\mapsto\langle F(z)x,y\rangle$ is [entire](c:entire-function) and bounded by $\|T\|\|x\|\|y\|$. By Liouville it is constant, so it equals $\langle Tx,y\rangle$. Hence $F(z)=T$ for all $z$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $F(z)=T$ at $z=0$ to obtain $N^*T=TN^*$.
steps.detail: The product rule gives $F'(0)=iN^*T-iTN^*$. Since $F$ is constant, $F'(0)=0$. So $N^*T=TN^*$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Inner products and adjoints let the proof use unitaries and scalar functions.
concepts.c:normal-operator: Normality makes $N$ and $N^*$ commute, so $U_z$ factors.
concepts.c:commutant: The hypothesis says that $T$ lies in the commutant of $N$.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: A unitary $U_z$ conjugates $T$ without changing its norm.
concepts.c:entire-function: Boundedness of the entire function $\langle F(z)x,y\rangle$ makes it constant.

source.note: M. Rosenblum, On a theorem of Fuglede and Putnam, J. London Math. Soc. 33 (1958) 376-377; the theorem is due to B. Fuglede (1950).

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth complete connected curve over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $0$. Let $G$ be a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) over $k$ with [Langlands dual group](c:langlands-dual-group) $\check G$. Then the Langlands functor is an equivalence $\mathrm{D\text{-}mod}_{1/2}(\mathrm{Bun}_G)\simeq\mathrm{IndCoh}_{\mathrm{Nilp}}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check G})$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $X$ is smooth, complete and connected over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $0$.
The group $G$ is connected and [reductive](c:reductive-group), with [Langlands dual](c:langlands-dual-group) $\check G$.

conclusion: The Langlands functor from half-twisted [D-modules](c:d-module) on the [moduli stack of bundles](c:moduli-stack-of-bundles) to ind-coherent sheaves with nilpotent singular support on the stack of [local systems](c:local-system) is an equivalence.

proofs.name: Gaitsgory-Raskin proof (outline)
proofs.slogan: Construct the Langlands functor, show that it respects Kac-Moody localization and Eisenstein series, treat the cuspidal part, and prove multiplicity one.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published five-paper proof for the de Rham form in characteristic $0$. Every step rests on the cited papers; the Betti form and the restricted and tempered forms are shown equivalent there.

roles.why: The curve $X$ supplies the formal discs for Kac-Moody localization and the Hecke action.
The reductive group $G$ and its parabolic subgroups give the Eisenstein and cuspidal pieces.

steps.slogan: Fix the automorphic and spectral categories of the conjecture.
steps.detail: The automorphic side is half-twisted [D-modules](c:d-module) on the [moduli stack of bundles](c:moduli-stack-of-bundles) for $G$. The spectral side is ind-coherent sheaves with nilpotent singular support on the stack of de Rham [local systems](c:local-system) for $\check G$, as formulated by Arinkin and Gaitsgory.

steps.slogan: Construct the Langlands functor from the automorphic side to the spectral side.
steps.detail: Paper I of the series builds the functor $\mathbb L_G$ in characteristic $0$ (de Rham and Betti settings) and proves its basic properties.

steps.slogan: Prove the fundamental local equivalence and link it with Kac-Moody localization.
steps.detail: Paper II proves the fundamental local equivalence at the critical level. It studies how Kac-Moody localization interacts with the global Langlands functor.

steps.slogan: Show that the functor commutes with Eisenstein series and constant terms.
steps.detail: Paper III proves that $\mathbb L_G$ is compatible with parabolic induction, that is with Eisenstein series and constant term functors. It deduces that $\mathbb L_G$ is an equivalence on the subcategories generated by Eisenstein series.

steps.slogan: Show that the functor is ambidextrous on the cuspidal category.
steps.detail: Paper IV proves that $\mathbb L_G$ restricted to the cuspidal category is ambidextrous. It also deduces the conjecture for $G=GL_n$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the functor is an equivalence by the multiplicity one theorem.
steps.detail: Paper V proves the multiplicity one theorem. Together with papers I to IV it shows that $\mathbb L_G$ is an equivalence.

concepts.c:reductive-group: The theorem is stated for a connected reductive group $G$.
concepts.c:langlands-dual-group: The spectral side uses local systems for the dual group $\check G$.
concepts.c:d-module: D-modules on the stack of bundles form the automorphic category.
concepts.c:moduli-stack-of-bundles: The stack $\mathrm{Bun}_G$ carries the automorphic category.
concepts.c:local-system: The stack of local systems carries the spectral category.

source.ref: D. Arinkin, D. Beraldo, J. Campbell, L. Chen, J. Faergeman, D. Gaitsgory, K. Lin, S. Raskin and N. Rozenblyum, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I-V (papers by subsets of these authors), arXiv:2405.03599, 2405.03648, 2409.07051, 2409.08670 and 2409.09856, 2024
source.note: I: construction of the functor; II: Kac-Moody localization and the FLE; III: compatibility with parabolic induction; IV: ambidexterity; V: the multiplicity one theorem. The conjecture is formulated in D. Arinkin and D. Gaitsgory, Singular support of coherent sheaves and the geometric Langlands conjecture, Selecta Math. 21 (2015).

statement: Let $E/\mathbb Q$ be an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) of conductor $N$. Let $K$ be an [imaginary quadratic field](c:imaginary-quadratic-field) of discriminant $D\ne-3,-4$ in which every prime divisor of $N$ splits. For the [Heegner point](c:heegner-point) $P_K\in E(K)$, $L'(E/K,1)=\dfrac{\|\omega\|^2}{c^2u^2\sqrt{|D|}}\,\hat h(P_K)$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $E/\mathbb Q$ has conductor $N$, Manin constant $c$ and Neron differential $\omega$, with $\|\omega\|^2=\int_{E(\mathbb C)}|\omega\wedge\bar\omega|$.
The field $K$ has discriminant $D\ne-3,-4$, every prime dividing $N$ splits in $K$, and $u=|\mathcal O_K^\times|/2$.

conclusion: The central derivative of the [L-function](c:l-function) of $E$ over $K$ equals $\|\omega\|^2/(c^2u^2\sqrt{|D|})$ times the Neron-Tate height $\hat h(P_K)$.

proofs.name: Gross-Zagier proof (outline)
proofs.slogan: Relate the central derivative to a Rankin-Selberg convolution, express the height of the Heegner class through local heights on the modular curve, and match the two series.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Gross-Zagier theorem for the trivial character, which is the formula that the record's alias names. The general formula for newforms and ring class characters is in the cited paper.

roles.why: The curve $E$ gives a newform $f$ and a modular parametrization that carries the formula down to $E$.
The field $K$ and the Heegner hypothesis give the Heegner points and the theta series of $K$.

steps.slogan: Attach the newform $f$ and the modular parametrization of $X_0(N)$ to $E$.
steps.detail: By the modularity theorem, $E$ is a quotient of the Jacobian of the [modular curve](c:modular-curve) $X_0(N)$ and has a weight $2$ newform $f$ with $L(E,s)=L(f,s)$. The Heegner hypothesis gives Heegner points on $X_0(N)$ with complex multiplication by $\mathcal O_K$. Their image in $E(K)$ gives $P_K$.

steps.slogan: Write the central derivative as a Petersson product by Rankin's method.
steps.detail: Gross and Zagier write $L(E/K,s)$ as a Rankin-Selberg convolution of $f$ with the theta series of $K$ (see the [Rankin-Selberg method](c:rankin-selberg-method)). They express its derivative at $s=1$ through a holomorphic projection that involves an incoherent Eisenstein series. They compute the Fourier coefficients of that projection.

steps.slogan: Split the height of the Heegner class into local height pairings.
steps.detail: On the Jacobian of $X_0(N)$, the height pairing of the Heegner class with its Hecke translates is a sum of local terms. Archimedean terms come from Green's functions. Non-archimedean terms come from intersection numbers of Heegner divisors on an integral model, computed by counting endomorphisms of supersingular curves.

steps.slogan: Match the Fourier coefficients of the height series and the Eisenstein projection.
steps.detail: Gross and Zagier show that the coefficients of the two generating series agree. Projection to the $f$-eigenspace, with multiplicity one for newforms, gives the formula for the height of the $f$-part of the Heegner class.

steps.slogan: Push the $f$-part of the Heegner class down to $E$ and collect the constants.
steps.detail: The modular parametrization maps the Heegner class to $P_K$. Its degree (through the Manin constant $c$), the period $\|\omega\|^2$, and the unit index $u$ give the constant in the formula for $\hat h(P_K)$.

concepts.c:elliptic-curve: The formula is about the curve $E$ and its Mordell-Weil point $P_K$.
concepts.c:imaginary-quadratic-field: The field $K$ carries the complex multiplication that defines the Heegner points.
concepts.c:heegner-point: The point $P_K$ is the image of the Heegner points of $X_0(N)$.
concepts.c:l-function: The derivative of $L(E/K,s)$ at $s=1$ is the analytic side of the formula.
concepts.c:modular-curve: The Heegner divisors and their heights live on the curve $X_0(N)$.
concepts.c:rankin-selberg-method: Rankin's method turns the $L$-function into a Petersson inner product.

source.ref: B. H. Gross and D. B. Zagier, Heegner points and derivatives of L-series, Inventiones Mathematicae 84 (1986), 225-320
source.note: The formula for elliptic curves is the case of the trivial character of the main theorem; it uses the modularity of E, now a theorem.

statement: Let $f_1,\dots,f_n$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) functions on $[0,1]$. Then there are points $0=z_0\le z_1\le\dots\le z_{n+1}=1$ with $\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j\int_{z_j}^{z_{j+1}}f_i=0$ for every $i=1,\dots,n$.

hypotheses.text: Each function $f_i$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[0,1]$.

conclusion: Some points $0=z_0\le\dots\le z_{n+1}=1$ make all $n$ alternating signed integrals $\sum_j(-1)^j\int_{z_j}^{z_{j+1}}f_i$ vanish.

proofs.name: Borsuk-Ulam on the sphere
proofs.slogan: Map a point of the sphere $S^n$ to the signed integrals over the partition it defines, and find a zero of this odd map by Borsuk-Ulam.
proofs.scope: The case $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ nothing is to prove. Zero-length intervals occur when a coordinate is $0$ and are allowed.

roles.why: Integrability makes each integral $\int_{z_j}^{z_{j+1}}f_i$ finite and continuous in the end points.

steps.slogan: Parametrize partitions and signs by a point of the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$.
steps.detail: For $x=(x_0,\dots,x_n)$ with $\sum x_j^2=1$, put $z_j=\sum_{k<j}x_k^2$. Then $0=z_0\le\dots\le z_{n+1}=1$. Give the interval $[z_j,z_{j+1}]$ the sign $\operatorname{sgn}(x_j)$.

steps.slogan: Define the map $\Phi\colon S^n\to\mathbb R^n$ by the signed integrals.
steps.detail: Let $\Phi_i(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\operatorname{sgn}(x_j)\int_{z_j}^{z_{j+1}}f_i$; each integral is continuous in its end points. An interval of length $x_j^2$ contributes $0$ in the limit $x_j\to0$, where $\operatorname{sgn}$ jumps. So $\Phi$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi$ is odd: $\Phi(-x)=-\Phi(x)$.
steps.detail: The point $-x$, the [antipodal](c:antipodal-map) point of $x$, has the same $z_j$ and opposite signs. So every signed integral changes its sign.

steps.slogan: Find a point $x\in S^n$ with $\Phi(x)=0$ by the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.
steps.detail: Borsuk-Ulam gives $x$ with $\Phi(x)=\Phi(-x)$ for the continuous map $\Phi\colon S^n\to\mathbb R^n$. Oddness gives $\Phi(-x)=-\Phi(x)$, so $\Phi(x)=0$.

steps.slogan: Merge equal neighboring signs and pad to alternating signs.
steps.detail: At the zero $x$, delete zero-length intervals and join neighbors of equal sign; the sums do not change. This leaves $m\le n+1$ intervals with alternating signs. Add zero-length intervals at $1$ up to $n+1$ intervals, and negate all signs if the first sign is $-$.

concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes the signed integrals finite and continuous in the end points.
concepts.c:sphere: The sphere $S^n$ parametrizes the partitions with their signs.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $\Phi$ is required by the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.
concepts.c:antipodal-map: The antipodal point reverses the signs, which makes $\Phi$ odd.

source.note: A. Pinkus, A simple proof of the Hobby-Rice theorem, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 60 (1976) 82-84; the theorem is from C. R. Hobby and J. R. Rice, A moment problem in L1 approximation, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 16 (1965) 665-670.

statement: Let $n\ge2$ agents choose efforts $a_i$ at costs $\psi_i(a_i)$ and share the output $x(a)$ by differentiable rules with $\sum_is_i(x)=x$. If an interior profile $a^*$ is [Pareto efficient](c:pareto-efficiency), that is, maximizes $x(a)-\sum_i\psi_i(a_i)$, with $\partial_ix(a^*)>0$, then $a^*$ is no [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium) of the payoffs $s_i(x(a))-\psi_i(a_i)$.

hypotheses.text: There are $n\ge2$ agents with efforts $a_i$ in open intervals, a differentiable output $x(a)$ and differentiable costs $\psi_i$.
The sharing rules $s_i$ are differentiable and balance the budget: $\sum_is_i(x)=x$ for all $x$.
The interior profile $a^*$ is [Pareto efficient](c:pareto-efficiency): it maximizes $x(a)-\sum_i\psi_i(a_i)$.
Every effort raises the output at $a^*$: $\partial_ix(a^*)>0$ for all $i$.

conclusion: The profile $a^*$ is not a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium): some agent gains by changing their effort.

proofs.name: First-order conditions and budget balance
proofs.slogan: Compare the first-order conditions of efficiency and of equilibrium, then sum the sharing-rule derivatives to contradict budget balance.
proofs.scope: The differentiable model of Holmstrom (1982) with interior efforts and $n\ge2$ agents. With transferable payoffs, Pareto efficiency of efforts means maximal total surplus.

roles.why: Open effort intervals and differentiability give first-order conditions for each agent.
The budget identity, once differentiated, forces the derivatives $s_i'$ to sum to $1$.
Efficiency of $a^*$ gives the condition $\partial_ix=\psi_i'$ for each agent.
A positive marginal product makes each marginal cost positive, so the ratio step is valid.

steps.slogan: Write the first-order conditions of efficiency at $a^*$.
steps.detail: The profile $a^*$ is interior and maximizes the differentiable surplus. So $\partial_ix(a^*)=\psi_i'(a_i^*)$ for each $i$. Since $\partial_ix(a^*)>0$, each $\psi_i'(a_i^*)$ is positive.

steps.slogan: Assume a Nash equilibrium and write the first-order condition of each agent.
steps.detail: Suppose $a^*$ is a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium). The payoff $s_i(x(a))-\psi_i(a_i)$ of agent $i$ is maximal at the interior point $a_i^*$. So $s_i'(x^*)\,\partial_ix(a^*)=\psi_i'(a_i^*)$ with $x^*=x(a^*)$.

steps.slogan: Combine both conditions to get $s_i'(x^*)=1$ for every agent.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give $s_i'(x^*)\,\partial_ix(a^*)=\partial_ix(a^*)$. Since $\partial_ix(a^*)>0$, we get $s_i'(x^*)=1$ for each $i$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the budget identity to get $\sum_is_i'(x^*)=1$.
steps.detail: The identity $\sum_is_i(x)=x$ holds for all $x$ and every $s_i$ is differentiable. So $\sum_is_i'(x)=1$ at every $x$, in particular at $x^*$.

steps.slogan: Sum the derivatives $s_i'(x^*)$ and contradict budget balance when $n\ge2$.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $\sum_is_i'(x^*)=n\ge2$, and step 4 gives $\sum_is_i'(x^*)=1$. This contradiction shows that $a^*$ is not a Nash equilibrium.

concepts.c:pareto-efficiency: Efficiency of $a^*$ gives the first-order condition $\partial_ix=\psi_i'$.
concepts.c:nash-equilibrium: The assumed equilibrium gives each agent's own first-order condition.

source.note: B. Holmstrom, Moral hazard in teams, Bell Journal of Economics 13 (1982) 324-340.

statement: Let $R$ and $B$ be finite sets of points in $\mathbb R^d$. If for every $S\subseteq R\cup B$ with $|S|\le d+2$ the sets $R\cap S$ and $B\cap S$ are strictly [linearly separable](c:linear-separability) by a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane), then $R$ and $B$ are strictly separable by a hyperplane.

hypotheses.text: The sets $R$ and $B$ are finite subsets of $\mathbb R^d$.
Every $S\subseteq R\cup B$ with $|S|\le d+2$ has $R\cap S$ and $B\cap S$ strictly separable by a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane).

conclusion: Some $u\in\mathbb R^d$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\langle u,r\rangle<t<\langle u,b\rangle$ for all $r\in R$ and $b\in B$.

proofs.name: Helly in the space of hyperplanes
proofs.slogan: Each point defines an open half-space of hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, any $d+2$ of these meet, so Helly's theorem gives a common hyperplane.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $R$ and $B$; the converse is clear, because subsets of separable sets are separable. If $R$ or $B$ is empty the claim is trivial.

roles.why: A finite family of convex sets is what Helly's theorem needs.
The local hypothesis shows that any $d+2$ half-spaces have a common hyperplane.

steps.slogan: Turn each point into an open half-space of pairs $(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$.
steps.detail: For $r\in R$ let $U_r=\{(u,t):\langle u,r\rangle<t\}$, and for $b\in B$ let $V_b=\{(u,t):\langle u,b\rangle>t\}$. A pair $(u,t)$ lies in all these sets exactly when the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $\{\langle u,\cdot\rangle=t\}$ strictly separates $R$ from $B$. Each set is open and [convex](c:convex-set).

steps.slogan: Show that any $d+2$ of these sets have a common point.
steps.detail: Choose $d+2$ of the sets, or all of them if there are fewer. They come from a set $S$ of at most $d+2$ points. By hypothesis a hyperplane separates $R\cap S$ from $B\cap S$, and its pair $(u,t)$ lies in the chosen sets.

steps.slogan: Obtain a common point of all the sets from Helly's theorem in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$.
steps.detail: The family is finite and consists of convex sets in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and any $d+2$ of its members meet by step 2. Helly's theorem gives a point common to all members.

steps.slogan: Read the common point as a separating hyperplane.
steps.detail: A common point $(u,t)$ satisfies $\langle u,r\rangle<t$ for all $r\in R$ and $\langle u,b\rangle>t$ for all $b\in B$. So its hyperplane strictly separates $R$ from $B$.

concepts.c:linear-separability: The theorem asks when two finite point sets are linearly separable.
concepts.c:hyperplane: A hyperplane $\{\langle u,\cdot\rangle=t\}$ is the object each pair $(u,t)$ encodes.
concepts.c:convex-set: Helly's theorem applies to the convex half-spaces of hyperplanes.

source.note: The standard Helly-type argument: hyperplanes are points of R^{d+1}, and each data point cuts out an open half-space of them.

statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite nonempty subsets of an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), and let $H=\{g:g+A+B=A+B\}$ be the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) of the [sumset](c:sumset) $A+B$. Then $|A+B|\ge|A+H|+|B+H|-|H|$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), written additively.
The sets $A$ and $B$ are finite and nonempty subsets of $G$.

conclusion: The inequality $|A+B|\ge|A+H|+|B+H|-|H|$ holds, where $H$ is the stabilizer of $A+B$.

proofs.name: Dyson transform proof (outline)
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a sumset with trivial stabilizer by a quotient, then run a minimal-counterexample argument with the Dyson e-transform.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the final comparison of periods is in the cited work. For trivial $H$ the bound reads $|A+B|\ge|A|+|B|-1$, and Cauchy-Davenport is the case $G=\mathbb Z/p$.

roles.why: Commutativity makes the quotient group and the translates $B+e$ behave as sets of sums.
Finiteness makes the sizes finite, so a counterexample of least size exists.

steps.slogan: Pass to the quotient by $H$ to reduce to a sumset with trivial stabilizer.
steps.detail: Let $\bar A,\bar B$ be the images in the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/H$. Then $|A+B|=|H|\,|\bar A+\bar B|$, $|A+H|=|H||\bar A|$ and $|B+H|=|H||\bar B|$. The sumset $\bar A+\bar B$ has trivial stabilizer, and the claim becomes $|\bar A+\bar B|\ge|\bar A|+|\bar B|-1$.

steps.slogan: Define the Dyson $e$-transform of the pair $(A,B)$ for $e\in A-B$.
steps.detail: Put $A(e)=A\cup(B+e)$ and $B(e)=B\cap(A-e)$. Then $B(e)\ne\emptyset$, since $e=a-b$ puts $b$ in it. Also $A(e)+B(e)\subseteq A+B$, and $|A(e)|+|B(e)|=|A|+|B|$ because $|A\cap(B+e)|=|(A-e)\cap B|$.

steps.slogan: Take a failing pair with the smallest sumset and then the largest $A$.
steps.detail: Suppose the bound fails for some pair with trivial stabilizer. Choose one with $|A+B|$ minimal and then $|A|$ maximal. For $e$ with $B(e)\ne B$, the transformed sumset is a strictly smaller subset of $A+B$, and it is periodic, since otherwise the transformed pair would also fail.

steps.slogan: Compare the period of the transformed sumset with the original pair.
steps.detail: The cited proof studies the stabilizer $K\ne0$ of $A(e)+B(e)$ for a well-chosen $e$. It shows that this periodicity contradicts the aperiodicity of $A+B$ or the choice of the pair in step 3.

steps.slogan: Conclude the aperiodic bound and transfer it back through the quotient.
steps.detail: No failing pair exists, so $|\bar A+\bar B|\ge|\bar A|+|\bar B|-1$ for trivial stabilizer. Step 1 turns this into $|A+B|\ge|A+H|+|B+H|-|H|$ in general.

concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity of $G$ makes sumsets, quotients and translates well behaved.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer $H$ of $A+B$ is the period that the quotient step removes.
concepts.c:sumset: The theorem bounds the size of the sumset $A+B$ from below.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The quotient $G/H$ reduces the general bound to trivial stabilizer.

source.ref: M. B. Nathanson, Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 165, Springer, 1996, Chapter 4 (Kneser's theorem for groups)
source.note: The theorem is due to M. Kneser (Math. Z. 58 (1953) and Math. Z. 66 (1956)); the book gives the e-transform proof.

statement: Let $G=\ast_{i\in I}G_i$ be a [free product](c:free-product) and $H\le G$ a subgroup. Then $H=F\ast\big(\ast_{j\in J}g_jA_jg_j^{-1}\big)$, where $F$ is a [free group](c:free-group), each $g_j\in G$, and each $A_j$ is a subgroup of some $G_i$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is the [free product](c:free-product) of the groups $G_i$, $i\in I$.
The group $H$ is a subgroup of $G$.

conclusion: The subgroup $H$ is the free product of a free group and of conjugates $g_jA_jg_j^{-1}$ of subgroups $A_j\le G_{i(j)}$.

proofs.name: Covering space of a wedge
proofs.slogan: Take the covering space of a wedge of spaces that belongs to $H$ and read its fundamental group from the pieces over each wedge summand and from a graph.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any index set $I$ and any factors $G_i$. The free factor $F$ comes from a graph, and the conjugates come from the components over the summands.

roles.why: The free product is the fundamental group of the wedge of spaces $X_i$.
The subgroup $H$ selects the covering space whose fundamental group is $H$.

steps.slogan: Build a wedge of connected complexes $X_i$ with fundamental groups $G_i$.
steps.detail: Choose connected [CW complexes](c:cw-complex) $X_i$ with $\pi_1(X_i)=G_i$, and let $X=\bigvee_iX_i$ be the [wedge sum](c:wedge-sum) at the point $x_0$. By the Seifert-van Kampen theorem, $\pi_1(X)=\ast_iG_i=G$.

steps.slogan: Take the connected covering space $p\colon\tilde X\to X$ with $p_*\pi_1(\tilde X)=H$.
steps.detail: A CW complex is locally contractible, so covering space theory gives a connected [covering space](c:covering-space) $\tilde X$ with base point $\tilde x_0$ and $p_*\pi_1(\tilde X,\tilde x_0)=H$.

steps.slogan: Identify the fundamental group of each component over a summand $X_i$.
steps.detail: Let $C$ be a component of $p^{-1}(X_i)$ and $\tilde x\in C$ a point over $x_0$, and let a path from $\tilde x_0$ to $\tilde x$ project to the loop $g\in G$. Then $p_*\pi_1(C,\tilde x)=g^{-1}Hg\cap G_i=:A$. Transported by $g$, it is the subgroup $gAg^{-1}=gG_ig^{-1}\cap H$ of $H$.

steps.slogan: Join the components through the lifts of $x_0$ into a connected graph $\Gamma$.
steps.detail: Let $\Gamma$ have one vertex for each component of each $p^{-1}(X_i)$ and one for each lift of $x_0$. Join a lift to each component that contains it. The space $\tilde X$ is connected and is the union of these components glued at the lifts, so $\Gamma$ is connected.

steps.slogan: Compute $\pi_1(\tilde X)$ as a free product of the pieces and the free group of $\Gamma$.
steps.detail: Choose a maximal tree in $\Gamma$ and apply the Seifert-van Kampen theorem repeatedly. Then $\pi_1(\tilde X)$ is the free product of the groups $gAg^{-1}$ of step 3 and the [free group](c:free-group) $\pi_1(\Gamma)$ on the edges outside the tree. This is $H$.

concepts.c:free-product: The group $G$ is a free product, and so is the result for $H$.
concepts.c:free-group: The fundamental group of the graph $\Gamma$ gives the free factor $F$.
concepts.c:cw-complex: CW complexes realize the groups $G_i$ and have good covering theory.
concepts.c:wedge-sum: The wedge of the spaces $X_i$ realizes the free product.
concepts.c:covering-space: The covering space of $X$ for $H$ carries the structure of $H$.

source.note: The covering-space proof, as in the Kurosh theorem treatments of Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Chapter 1; a Bass-Serre tree proof is in J.-P. Serre, Trees, Chapter I.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) and $\alpha\in H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ a class whose image in $H^2(X,\mathbb C)$ has type $(1,1)$ in the [Hodge decomposition](c:hodge-decomposition). Then $\alpha=c_1(L)$ for some holomorphic [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ on $X$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $X$ is compact and [Kähler](c:kahler-manifold).
The class $\alpha$ lies in $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$.
The image of $\alpha$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb C)$ lies in $H^{1,1}(X)$, the middle part of the [Hodge decomposition](c:hodge-decomposition).

conclusion: A holomorphic line bundle $L$ on $X$ has first Chern class $c_1(L)=\alpha$.

proofs.name: Exponential sheaf sequence
proofs.slogan: Use the exponential sequence to see that $\alpha$ is a Chern class exactly when its image in $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)$ vanishes, and Hodge theory to check this for type $(1,1)$.
proofs.scope: The direct implication: every integral $(1,1)$-class is a Chern class. The converse holds because the curvature form of a hermitian metric on $L$ is a closed $(1,1)$-form that represents $c_1(L)$.

roles.why: The Kähler condition gives the Hodge decomposition and the identification of $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)$ with $H^{0,2}$.
Integrality lets $\alpha$ lie in the term $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ of the long exact sequence.
Type $(1,1)$ means that the $(0,2)$-component of $\alpha$ is zero.

steps.slogan: Write the exponential sequence of sheaves on $X$.
steps.detail: The sequence $0\to\underline{\mathbb Z}\to\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)}\mathcal O_X^*\to0$ is exact. A nonvanishing holomorphic function has a local logarithm, unique up to adding an element of $\mathbb Z$. See the [exponential exact sequence](c:exponential-exact-sequence).

steps.slogan: Take cohomology to characterize the Chern classes of line bundles.
steps.detail: The [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) sequence contains $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)\xrightarrow{c_1}H^2(X,\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{j}H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)$. The group $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)$ classifies line bundles, and the connecting map is the [first Chern class](c:first-chern-class). So $\alpha=c_1(L)$ for some $L$ exactly when $j(\alpha)=0$.

steps.slogan: Factor $j$ through $H^2(X,\mathbb C)$ and the projection to $H^{0,2}$.
steps.detail: The map $j$ comes from $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb C\subset\mathcal O_X$, so it factors through $H^2(X,\mathbb C)$. Dolbeault's theorem gives $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)\cong H^{0,2}(X)$. On a compact Kähler manifold the map $H^2(X,\mathbb C)\to H^{0,2}(X)$ is the projection of the Hodge decomposition.

steps.slogan: Show that a class of type $(1,1)$ has zero $(0,2)$-component.
steps.detail: By hypothesis the image of $\alpha$ in $H^2(X,\mathbb C)$ lies in $H^{1,1}(X)$. So its projection to $H^{0,2}(X)$ is zero, and $j(\alpha)=0$.

steps.slogan: Use exactness to find a line bundle with first Chern class $\alpha$.
steps.detail: Since $j(\alpha)=0$, exactness at $H^2(X,\mathbb Z)$ gives a class $L\in H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)$ with $c_1(L)=\alpha$.

concepts.c:kahler-manifold: The Kähler condition supplies the Hodge decomposition used to compute $j$.
concepts.c:hodge-decomposition: Type $(1,1)$ is a statement about the Hodge decomposition of $H^2$.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The conclusion says that $\alpha$ is the Chern class of a line bundle.
concepts.c:exponential-exact-sequence: The sequence relates integral cohomology to holomorphic line bundles.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The long exact sequence in sheaf cohomology contains the Chern class map.
concepts.c:first-chern-class: The connecting map of the sequence is the first Chern class.

source.note: Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry, Chapter 1 (the Lefschetz theorem on (1,1) classes); also Voisin, Hodge Theory and Complex Algebraic Geometry I, Chapter 7.

statement: The [alternating series](c:alternating-series) $\sum_{i\ge0}(-1)^i/(2i+1)$ converges, and its sum is $\pi/4$.
conclusion: The partial sums $\sum_{i<k}(-1)^i/(2i+1)$ converge to $\pi/4$ as $k\to\infty$.

proofs.name: Abel's theorem and the arctangent series
proofs.slogan: Extend the arctangent series to $y=1$ by Abel's limit theorem, and read off $\arctan1=\pi/4$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. The series first converges by the alternating series test, and only then is its sum identified.

steps.slogan: Show that the series converges to some limit $l$.
steps.detail: The terms $1/(2i+1)$ decrease to $0$. By the alternating series test, the partial sums converge to a limit $l$.

steps.slogan: Apply Abel's limit theorem to get $\sum a_ix^i\to l$ as $x\to1^-$.
steps.detail: Abel's limit theorem says that if $\sum a_i$ converges to $l$, then the [power series](c:power-series) $\sum a_ix^i$ tends to $l$ as $x\to1^-$. Here $a_i=(-1)^i/(2i+1)$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\sum(-1)^iy^{2i+1}/(2i+1)$ with $\arctan y$ for $|y|<1$.
steps.detail: For $|t|<1$ the geometric series gives $1/(1+t^2)=\sum(-1)^it^{2i}$, uniformly on compact subsets. Integrating term by term from $0$ to $y$ gives the series of the [arctangent](c:arctangent): $\arctan y=\sum(-1)^iy^{2i+1}/(2i+1)$.

steps.slogan: Let $y\to1^-$ to show that $\arctan y\to l$.
steps.detail: For $0<y<1$ put $x=y^2$; step 3 gives $\arctan y=y\sum a_ix^i$. As $y\to1^-$, also $x\to1^-$ and $y\to1$, so step 2 gives $\arctan y\to l$.

steps.slogan: Compare with the continuity of $\arctan$ at $1$ to get $l=\pi/4$.
steps.detail: Since $\arctan$ is continuous, $\arctan y\to\arctan1=\pi/4$ as $y\to1^-$. Limits are unique, so $l=\pi/4$.

concepts.c:alternating-series: The series alternates with decreasing terms, so it converges.
concepts.c:power-series: Abel's theorem controls the power series near the end of its interval.
concepts.c:arctangent: The arctangent has this power series, and its value at $1$ is $\pi/4$.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [solvable](c:solvable-group) linear [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) over an algebraically closed field $k$, and $\rho\colon G\to GL(V)$ a rational representation on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $V$. Then some line $L\subseteq V$ is invariant: $\rho(g)L=L$ for all $g\in G$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a connected [solvable](c:solvable-group) linear [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group).
The field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The map $\rho\colon G\to GL(V)$ is a rational representation on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $V$.

conclusion: Some line $L\subseteq V$ satisfies $\rho(g)L=L$ for all $g\in G$.

proofs.name: Induction on the derived length
proofs.slogan: Reduce to an irreducible module, show that the commutator subgroup acts trivially, and find a common eigenvector of the commuting action that remains.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Induction on $\dim V$ then gives a basis in which $\rho(G)$ is upper triangular.

roles.why: Connectedness and solvability give a connected commutator subgroup of smaller derived length and no finite-index closed subgroups.
An algebraically closed field gives common eigenvectors of commuting operators.
Rationality makes the stabilizers closed and the weights morphisms to $k^*$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a minimal nonzero invariant subspace $W$ of $V$.
steps.detail: Choose a nonzero $G$-stable subspace $W\subseteq V$ of least dimension. Then $W$ is an [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation), and an invariant line in $W$ is one in $V$. We induct on the derived length of $G$, over all representations.

steps.slogan: Find a nonzero weight space $W_\chi$ of the commutator subgroup $G'$.
steps.detail: The [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) $G'$ is closed, connected and solvable of smaller derived length. If $G'=1$, go to step 6. Otherwise induction gives a $G'$-invariant line in $W$, hence a character $\chi$ of $G'$ with $W_\chi=\{w:hw=\chi(h)w\ \forall h\in G'\}\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G$ permutes the weight spaces of $G'$.
steps.detail: The group $G'$ is normal in $G$. For $g\in G$, $w\in W_\chi$ and $h\in G'$, $h(gw)=g(g^{-1}hg)w=\chi(g^{-1}hg)\,gw$. So $gW_\chi=W_{\chi^g}$ with $\chi^g(h)=\chi(g^{-1}hg)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G$ fixes $W_\chi$, so that $W=W_\chi$.
steps.detail: Weight spaces of distinct characters are independent, so $G$ permutes finitely many spaces. The stabilizer of $W_\chi$ is closed of finite index, hence equal to the connected group $G$. So $W_\chi$ is $G$-stable, and irreducibility gives $W_\chi=W$.

steps.slogan: Show that the commutator subgroup $G'$ acts trivially on $W$.
steps.detail: On $W=W_\chi$ each $h\in G'$ acts as the scalar $\chi(h)$. The determinant is trivial on commutators, so $\chi(h)^{\dim W}=1$. A character of the connected group $G'$ with values in the finite group of $\dim W$-th roots of unity is trivial.

steps.slogan: Find a common eigenvector of the commuting operators $\rho(G)$ on $W$.
steps.detail: Now $\rho$ acts on $W$ through the abelian group $G/G'$, so $\rho(G)$ is a commuting family of operators. Over the [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) field $k$ it has a common [eigenvector](c:eigenvector). Its span is an invariant line.

concepts.c:solvable-group: Solvability allows induction on the derived length of $G$.
concepts.c:algebraic-group: Algebraic structure makes commutator subgroups and stabilizers closed.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: It guarantees eigenvectors for the commuting operators.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility forces $G$-stable subspaces to be $0$ or all of $W$.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The commutator subgroup $G'$ is the smaller group handled by induction.
concepts.c:eigenvector: A common eigenvector spans the invariant line.

source.note: J. E. Humphreys, Linear Algebraic Groups, Theorem 17.6 (Lie-Kolchin); the proof follows its induction on the derived length.
